questions.marksProvenance: Not verified: source gives section totals only, without explicit individual-question or item allocations.
questions.answerKey: For the usual school example, baker’s yeast (Saccharomyces): Kingdom Fungi; Phylum/Division Ascomycota. Yeasts are not a single taxonomic group; some belong to Basidiomycota, so species clarification is required for a unique modern classification.

questions.content: Describe the mechanism of taking air into the human lungs.
questions.marksProvenance: Not verified: source gives section totals only, without explicit individual-question or item allocations.
questions.answerKey: During inhalation, the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs and sternum upwards and outwards. The diaphragm contracts and flattens downward. Thoracic volume increases and the lungs expand with the thoracic wall. Intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows through the airways into the lungs. These linked actions explain inspiration rather than gaseous diffusion across the alveolar wall.

questions.content: Briefly explain five ways of transmitting Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
questions.marksProvenance: Not verified: source gives section totals only, without explicit individual-question or item allocations.
questions.answerKey: Examples of five exposure routes: unprotected vaginal or anal sexual contact with an infected person; transfusion of infected unscreened blood; sharing contaminated injection needles or syringes; unsafe piercing, tattooing or cutting with instruments contaminated by infected blood; and transmission from an infected parent to a child during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding. HIV is not transmitted by ordinary touching, sharing food, or mosquito bites.

questions.content: In six points, support the statement that “Bacteria are important organisms to human being.”
questions.marksProvenance: Source cover page 1 gives Section C 15 marks; page 10 shows Question 10 is its only question.
questions.markIncrementProvenance: Independent whole-mark self-assessment rubric within the verified 15-mark question maximum; not an official NECTA subpart scheme.
questions.answerKey: Six beneficial roles include decomposition and nutrient recycling; nitrogen fixation that improves soil fertility; fermentation in food production such as yoghurt; useful gut bacteria that assist normal intestinal function and synthesise some vitamins; treatment of sewage and biodegradation of suitable wastes; and production of useful medicines or biotechnology products such as insulin by engineered bacteria. Explain each role and its benefit to people rather than merely naming bacteria.
questions.markingGuide: Verified source maximum: 15 marks because Question 10 is the only Section C question. Independently prepared self-assessment allocation, not official NECTA marking: 1 mark for a relevant introduction identifying bacteria as microorganisms with useful roles; 2 marks for each of six distinct explained beneficial roles (1 for the valid role and 1 for a clear explanation/example, maximum 12); 1 mark for coherent organisation; 1 mark for a relevant concluding statement. Accept other scientifically valid explained roles; do not count one role twice.

questions.verificationScope: All eleven original source pages visually inspected. Printed wording, full stems/options, labels, tables and question relationships preserved; original pages are authoritative.
questions.sourceContent: In six points, support the statement that “Bacteria are important organisms to human being.”
questions.curriculumCompatibilityNote: Compatible ecosystem/nutrition applications of microorganisms; the legacy paper is not a claim of current full syllabus coverage.
questions.workedSolution: Bacteria are microscopic organisms, many of which benefit humans. (1) Decomposing bacteria break down dead material and return mineral nutrients to ecosystems. (2) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, such as those associated with legume root nodules, convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds plants can use, supporting farming. (3) Lactic-acid bacteria ferment milk to make yoghurt and other foods. (4) Normal intestinal bacteria contribute to intestinal function and produce some vitamins, although bacterial roles and health effects vary. (5) Suitable bacteria break down organic matter during sewage treatment and can help degrade pollutants. (6) Bacteria are used in biotechnology to manufacture useful products, including insulin from genetically engineered strains. These examples show how bacterial activities support food production, health, industry and environmental management. This is an independent model answer, not a recovered official marking scheme.

verificationNotes: All eleven pages of the original source were visually inspected. Page 11 is continuation answer space only. Assessment-number lines, assessor boxes, answer boxes and ruled response lines remain in the complete source pages; question wording, choices, matching data, full shared experimental stems and report-table headers are transcribed.
No associated answer guide is available for this source. All model answers and rubrics are independently prepared, with no official NECTA solution provenance asserted.

The cover gives section totals A15/B70/C15 only. The ten MCQs and five matching items do not explicitly state per-item marks; Section B does not explicitly say each main question carries 10. No equal allocation is invented. All A/B questions therefore remain draft pending actual mark evidence.
Question 10 is the only Section C question, so its maximum 15 is verified directly. Only the internal rubric is independently prepared, clearly labelled.
The printed spelling/grammar, such as carbondioxide, indigested, a starch, warnings signs and human being, is retained. Scientific explanations in answers do not replace or edit question wording.

Question 1(x) arrow options are transcribed with the same organism order and rightward arrows; the complete original figure is also shown. Q8 report headers and Q9 blank labelled pictogram boxes are preserved, with complete original pages available.
The source Question 9(b) asks about three chemicals but prints response sublabels only for Flammable and Toxic. The missing third response label is not silently added.
The generic source word Yeast does not state species. A conventional Saccharomyces classification is explained conditionally; the wider modern taxonomic ambiguity remains recorded, not hidden.
